title: Increased sociality has benefits but also costs for burying beetles in a harsh environment
content:
Abstract
The harsh environment hypothesis posits that sociality should preferentially evolve in extreme or unpredictable environments. Although comparative studies largely support this trend, it is becoming clear that there are multiple reasons underlying this pattern that may differ from system to system. Therefore, targeted behavioral experiments are needed to identify the precise costs and benefits of sociality in harsh environments in a wide variety of contexts. Here, we perform a series of experiments focused on wet soil as a harsh environment for the burying beetle Nicrophorus orbicollis, a model system for the study of biparental care. We confirm previous work that wet soil presents a challenging but usable breeding environment for this species by showing that young pairs choose not to reproduce while several old pairs did so successfully. We show that the costs of breeding in this environment accrue primarily to larvae, who suffer high mortality prior to eclosion, especially when they are larger. We next show that increased sociality, both in the form of biparental care and biparental care with older partners, increase the likelihood of reproduction in wet soil, but does not increase the fitness of larvae. We lastly show that even dramatic reductions of parental care do not affect the fitness of larvae in wet soil. We argue that increased effort from social partners only benefits each other by reducing costs associated with breeding. However, the increased mortality of larger individuals suggests the surprising potential for a negative association between sociality and harsh environments.
